title: Electric circuits
description: Animated KS3 Physics lesson on electric circuits for ages 9 to 14: circuit symbols, complete circuits, conductors and insulators, current and ammeters, potential difference and voltmeters, series and parallel circuits, and resistance with R = V ÷ I.
intro: Circuit symbols, current, voltage, series and parallel circuits and resistance, explained by the owl in six short parts.

steps.say: A simple circuit needs a **cell** to push the current, **wires** to carry it, and a **component** such as a bulb.
In circuit diagrams we draw **symbols**. Here are the symbols for a cell, a bulb, a switch and a wire. The long line of the cell is its positive side.
Current can only flow round a **complete loop** with no gaps. The switch is closed, so the bulb lights up.
Open the switch and you make a **gap**. The circuit is broken, so no current flows and the bulb goes out.
Current flows easily through **conductors**, like copper and other metals. **Insulators**, like plastic and rubber, stop it. That's why wires are covered in plastic.

check.q: A circuit has a cell, a bulb and an **open** switch. Does the bulb light?
options: No, because the circuit is not a complete loop
Yes, because the cell is still connected
No, because the cell is the wrong way round
check.hint: Current needs a complete loop with no gaps. What does an open switch make?
check.explain: An open switch makes a **gap**, so the circuit is not complete. No current flows anywhere in the loop, so the bulb stays **off**.

steps.say: **Current** is a flow of electric **charge** round the circuit. A bigger current makes the same bulb glow more brightly.
We measure current in **amps** (A) with an **ammeter**. Its symbol is a circle with an A inside.
steps.speak: We measure current in amps, with an ammeter. Its symbol is a circle with the letter A inside.

steps.say: An ammeter goes **in series**: right in the loop, so all the current flows through it. This one reads 0.2 A.
steps.speak: An ammeter goes in series: right in the loop, so all the current flows through it. This one reads nought point two amps.

steps.say: We say current flows out of the **positive** side of the cell (the long line), round the circuit, and back into the **negative** side (the short line).
In a metal wire, the charges that really move are tiny **electrons**. They are negative, so they drift the other way: from negative to positive.

check.q: Which meter measures current, and how is it connected?
check.hint: A for amps. And all the current must flow through the meter, so it goes in the loop itself.
check.explain: Current is measured with an **ammeter**, in amps. It goes **in series**, in the loop, so all the current flows through it.

steps.say: The cell gives the charges a push, and they carry energy to the bulb. The size of this push is the **potential difference**, also called the **voltage**.
Potential difference is measured in **volts** (V) with a **voltmeter**. Its symbol is a circle with a V inside.
steps.speak: Potential difference is measured in volts, with a voltmeter. Its symbol is a circle with the letter V inside.

steps.say: A voltmeter is connected **in parallel**: across the bulb, with one wire on each side of it.
One cell gives about 1.5 V. Two cells joined in a line give 3 V. The bigger push makes a bigger current, so the bulb is brighter.
steps.speak: One cell gives about 1.5 volts. Two cells joined in a line give 3 volts. The bigger push makes a bigger current, so the bulb is brighter.

check.q: How should you connect a voltmeter to measure the potential difference across a bulb?
options: In series, next to the bulb
check.hint: A voltmeter compares the two sides of the bulb, so it needs a wire on each side.
check.explain: A voltmeter goes **in parallel**, across the bulb, with one wire each side. Ammeters go in series; voltmeters go across.

steps.say: In a **series circuit**, everything is joined in one loop. There is only one path for the current.
The current is the **same everywhere** in a series circuit. Every ammeter here reads 0.2 A.
steps.speak: The current is the same everywhere in a series circuit. Every ammeter here reads nought point two amps.

steps.say: The potential difference is **shared** between the bulbs. Two cells give 3 V, so two identical bulbs get 1.5 V each.
steps.speak: The potential difference is shared between the bulbs. Two cells give 3 volts, so two identical bulbs get 1.5 volts each.

steps.say: Add another bulb in series and the current gets smaller, so every bulb is **dimmer**.
If one bulb breaks, it leaves a gap in the only path. The current stops and **all** the bulbs go out.

check.q: Three bulbs are in series. The ammeter next to the cell reads 0.3 A. What is the current through the last bulb?
check.hint: In a series circuit there is only one path. Is the current used up as it goes round?
check.explain: In a series circuit the current is **the same everywhere**, so it is **0.3 A** through every bulb. Current is not used up; energy is what the bulbs take.

steps.say: In a **parallel circuit**, the current splits into separate **branches**. Each bulb has its own loop back to the cell.
The currents in the branches **add up** to the current from the cell. These bulbs are identical: 0.3 A + 0.3 A = 0.6 A.
steps.speak: The currents in the branches add up to the current from the cell. These bulbs are identical: nought point three amps plus nought point three amps equals nought point six amps.

steps.say: If one bulb breaks, the other branch is still a complete loop, so the other bulb **stays on**.
That's why the lights in a house are wired in parallel. Each light has its own switch, so one can be off while the others stay on.

check.q: A parallel circuit has two branches. One branch ammeter reads 0.2 A and the other reads 0.3 A. What does the ammeter next to the cell read?
check.hint: All the current from the cell splits up into the branches, then joins up again. So add the branches.
check.explain: The branch currents add up to the current from the cell: 0.2 + 0.3 = **0.5 A**.

steps.say: **Resistance** tells you how hard it is for current to flow through something. A **resistor** adds resistance. Its symbol is a rectangle.
Resistance is measured in **ohms** (Ω). With the same cells, more resistance means **less current**.
steps.speak: Resistance is measured in ohms. With the same cells, more resistance means less current.

steps.say: To work out resistance: **resistance = potential difference ÷ current**, or R = V ÷ I.
steps.speak: To work out resistance: resistance equals potential difference divided by current, or R equals V divided by I.

steps.say: This resistor has 6 V across it and 2 A through it. R = 6 ÷ 2 = 3 Ω.
steps.speak: This resistor has 6 volts across it and 2 amps through it. R equals 6 divided by 2, which is 3 ohms.

steps.say: You can turn it round to find the potential difference: V = I × R. A current of 4 A through 3 Ω needs 4 × 3 = 12 V.
steps.speak: You can turn it round to find the potential difference: V equals I times R. A current of 4 amps through 3 ohms needs 4 times 3, which is 12 volts.

check.q: A resistor has a potential difference of 12 V across it and a current of 3 A through it. What is its resistance? (R = V ÷ I)
check.hint: Divide the potential difference by the current. Don't multiply or add them.
